metadata.title: Students' and schools' expectancy-value beliefs are associated with reading achievement: A cross-cultural study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata and applies final student weights to adjust for unequal sampling selection chances, as stated in the Data analysis section (Mplus MG-CFA and doubly-latent ML-SEM used final student weights). The analytic sample is restricted to students in the specified Eastern and Western culture groups and to the PISA reading literacy domain, with expectancy/value measured via PISA self-report items. Missingness on questionnaire items is handled via MCMC imputation before model estimation, and all items are standardized to zero mean and unit SD. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the modeling approach is SEM-based rather than ML; therefore, the manuscript does not discuss how complex-survey variance estimation is implemented beyond the use of final student weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of PISA 2018 reading literacy data for 15-year-old students. The sample is partitioned into Eastern cultures (Mainland China, Hong Kong SAR, Macau SAR, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan) and Western cultures (USA, UK, Canada, New Zealand, Australia), with total counts reported as 41,872 and 61,755 respectively. The models use expectancy (reading self-concept) and value (intrinsic value/enjoyment) measured from PISA self-report items, and reading achievement is modeled using all 10 plausible values for reading. Missing item responses are imputed using MCMC, and the SEM estimation uses final student weights.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds), Eastern cultures (CHN, HKG, MAC, TWN, KOR, JPN)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Doubly-latent ML-SEM (student level): expectancy → reading achievement β = 0.33 (p < .001); value → reading achievement β = 0.29 (p < .001). School level: school expectancy → reading achievement β = 0.25 (p < .001); school value → reading achievement β = 0.18 (p < .001). Model fit indices for two-level model: CFI = 0.98, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.01, SRMRwithin = 0.02, SRMRbetween = 0.07. Variance explained: 20.8% of reading achievement variance at student level in Eastern cultures.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy data for Eastern cultures, the study leveraged reading self-concept (expectancy) and intrinsic value (value), alongside socioeconomic status and demographic covariates, to predict reading achievement (Plausible Values), finding that both student-level expectancy (β = 0.33) and value (β = 0.29) were positively associated with reading achievement and that school-level expectancy (β = 0.25) and value (β = 0.18) were also significant. This indicates that strengthening both students’ reading self-concept and intrinsic enjoyment, and improving the motivational climate at the school level, may be particularly important for reading achievement in Eastern contexts, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds), Western cultures (USA, GBR, CAN, NZL, AUS)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Doubly-latent ML-SEM (student level): expectancy → reading achievement β = 0.41 (p < .001); value → reading achievement β = 0.36 (p < .001). School level: school expectancy → reading achievement β = 0.02 (p > .05); school value → reading achievement β = −0.008 (p > .05). Two-level model fit indices: CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.97, RMSEA = 0.01, SRMRwithin = 0.02, SRMRbetween = 0.05. Variance explained: 35.2% of reading achievement variance at student level in Western cultures.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy data for Western cultures, the study leveraged reading self-concept (expectancy) and intrinsic value (value), alongside socioeconomic status and demographic covariates, to predict reading achievement (Plausible Values), finding that student-level expectancy (β = 0.41) and value (β = 0.36) were positively associated with reading achievement while school-level expectancy (β = 0.02) and school-level value (β = −0.008) were not significant. This indicates that interventions in Western contexts may need to prioritize individual motivational beliefs for reading rather than relying on school-level motivational climate effects, while recognizing that the study’s cross-sectional PISA design prevents causal inference.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds), cross-cultural multi-group comparison (Eastern vs Western)
main_findings.target_variable: Cross-cultural differences in expectancy/value paths to reading achievement
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multi-group multi-level SEM: school-level non-invariant relations χ2(138) = 141.02 (p < .001); student-level non-invariant relations χ2(138) = 850.83 (p < .001). Reported pattern: school-level expectancy/value more strongly associated with reading achievement in the East than in the West; student-level expectancy/value associations larger in the West than in the East.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading literacy the study leveraged expectancy (reading self-concept) and value (intrinsic value) to test whether their associations with reading achievement generalize across cultures, finding statistically significant cross-cultural differences in both student-level and school-level path magnitudes (student-level χ2(138) = 850.83, p < .001; school-level χ2(138) = 141.02, p < .001). This indicates that reading-motivation interventions should be culturally tailored—emphasizing school motivational climate in Eastern contexts and individual motivational beliefs in Western contexts—while noting that these are predictive associations from cross-sectional data rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2018 reading literacy for 15-year-olds, comparing Eastern cultures (Mainland China, Hong Kong SAR, Macau SAR, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan; n = 41,872) and Western cultures (USA, UK, Canada, New Zealand, Australia; n = 61,755). Expectancy is operationalized as reading self-concept and value as intrinsic value, both modeled with a two-factor measurement structure and tested for measurement invariance across 11 countries and across student vs school levels. Reading achievement is modeled using all 10 plausible values, estimated ten times and combined using Rubin’s method. Using doubly-latent multilevel structural equation modeling, student-level expectancy and value show positive associations with reading achievement in both cultures (Eastern β = 0.33/0.29; Western β = 0.41/0.36), while school-level expectancy/value are significant only in the East (β = 0.25/0.18) and not in the West (β = 0.02/−0.008). The study uses MCMC imputation for missing items and applies final student weights; however, the cross-sectional PISA design limits causal interpretation.
